title: Dental unit waterlines: biofilm, flushing and water quality
audience: Cleaners and assistants who work around dental units and need to recognise and report waterline faults.
learningOutcomes: Explain why biofilm forms inside dental unit water tubing.
Describe the controls that keep waterlines in a safe state.
Report a waterline fault without handling or dosing the water system.

instruction.heading: Why waterlines need attention
instruction.body: The narrow tubes that feed the handpieces, the three-way syringe and the ultrasonic scalers carry water slowly, and their inner surface is large compared with the volume they hold. Under those conditions, organisms from the environment can settle and build a film called biofilm. The film can release organisms into the water sprayed on patients and staff. Among the organisms the source flags from waterlines are Pseudomonas aeruginosa, one group of atypical mycobacteria, and Legionella. Biofilm is therefore regarded as a store of contamination, not as a nuisance.

instruction.heading: Water quality targets
instruction.body: The source asks that water used to cool or irrigate during tooth preparation and scaling meet at least the national drinking-water standard. It sets a bacterial count limit for coolant water in non-surgical work, and a tighter limit when care is given to people whose immune defences are weakened. Surgical procedures use sterile water or saline. Test results are checked against those limits.

instruction.heading: Keeping the lines in a safe state
instruction.body: The main controls are flushing the lines after each patient and again at the opening of each day, flushing after a long break, fitting anti-retraction valves so that fluid from the mouth cannot travel back into the lines, and treating the water by a method the manufacturer approves. Any treatment product is handled under the manufacturer's directions by a person trained to do it. A cleaner does not mix, dose or connect a water treatment product unless the role and training specifically allow it. Valves cannot stand in for flushing, and flushing cannot stand in for valves.

instruction.heading: Your part
instruction.body: A cleaner reports leaking lines, missing or damaged valves, a test kit past its use date, or water that looks or tastes unusual at the chair. A cleaner does not disconnect a line or interfere with a valve.

procedure: Check that the team has recorded the day's waterline flushing.
Confirm that anti-retraction valves are in place on any handpiece or scaler you can see.
Report leaks, damaged valves and out-of-date test kits to the practice manager or the dental nurse.
Do not mix, dose or connect any water treatment product unless you are trained for it and the role lists it.
Record the report with the chair or room and the time.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner notices a test kit left on the bench with a use date that has passed, and the water in the sample looks cloudy.
workedExamples.reasoning: Set the kit and the sample aside, and do not rely on either for any decision. Report the out-of-date kit and the cloudy sample to the practice manager or the dental nurse, and record the time.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked to top up the water treatment bottle on each chair.
workedExamples.reasoning: Only if the role includes it and the person is trained for that product. Otherwise refer the request, because dosing is a controlled task under the manufacturer's directions.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves when handling any chairside component
Manufacturer's instructions for the dental unit
Eye protection when a water treatment product is being used by someone trained for it

commonErrors.error: Assuming dental unit water is sterile because it comes from the tap.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat unit water as a reservoir that needs flushing and testing.

commonErrors.error: Removing or bypassing an anti-retraction valve to get better flow.
commonErrors.prevention: Report the damaged valve. Never remove it.

commonErrors.error: Dosing a line with a product that is not the one the manufacturer lists.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the listed product, under the practice protocol.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Water treatment products are chemicals. Follow the label, the safety data sheet and the PPE listed for them.
Dental unit water and sterilisers are maintained by trained staff. The cleaner's role here is to report, not to repair or treat.
The source names Australian standards and state rules.

qualityStandard: Each waterline fault the cleaner sees is reported the same shift.
No water treatment product is added to a line by an untrained person.
documentationEvidence: Waterline flushing record completed by the team
Report of any fault, with the chair or room and the time
summary: Waterlines hold biofilm because they are thin and slow-flowing, so they need routine flushing and testing.
The cleaner reports faults and never doses or disconnects the water system.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does biofilm build up inside a dental unit's water tubing?
options: Thin, long lines carry water slowly and have a large inner surface, so organisms settle.
The lines are too wide for water to flow and the flow is fast in every case.
The water is kept too cold for the unit's own pump and the pump runs all day long.
Dental water is sterile when it leaves the tap and nothing can grow in it later.

knowledgeChecks.question: What do anti-retraction valves do?
options: They help stop fluid from the mouth flowing back into the lines.
They are only decorative and they can be ignored by staff.
They can be removed to speed up flushing and the lines are cleaner after.
They can stand in for flushing and a quick rinse will do.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaner notices that a water-line test kit is out of date. What should they do?
options: Use it for one more week today, since the lines look clean enough
Report it to the practice manager or dental nurse, and do not dose the lines.
Fill the kit with water from the kitchen tap and then use the kit anyway
Remove the affected line and cap the end of the tube with tape today

sourceReferences: ADA Guidelines for Infection Control, 3rd ed. (Australian Dental Association, 2015), section C.2 (waterlines and water quality) and the note on flushing and biofilm; rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)

Cross-checked against the Malaysian Dental Council guideline section 4.2.1 (dental unit waterlines). The Malaysian flushing durations are not used; the Malaysian guideline sets timing the ADA does not. Both sources point to manufacturer directions. Source priority: the Australian NHMRC guideline, as summarised in HCG-01 to HCG-20, governs where it conflicts with this source.
The numeric bacterial limits and the drinking-water standard are not confirmed as current (UNCONFIRMED).
The source names Australian standards and state rules. Those are named only, and their current text is UNCONFIRMED here.
